identity.title: Fast Escape, Slow Convergence: Learning Dynamics of Phase Retrieval under Power-Law Data

problem.claim: Analyze scaling laws and learning dynamics in phase retrieval with anisotropic Gaussian inputs whose covariance spectrum follows a power law.

gap.claim: The isotropic two-dimensional description does not extend directly: anisotropy produces an infinite hierarchy of coupled equations, and the abstract presents a rigorous characterization for this nonlinear anisotropic setting as previously unavailable.

contributions.claim: Develops a tractable reduction of the anisotropic dynamics into three phases: fast escape, slow summary-statistic convergence, and spectral-tail learning.
Derives explicit mean-squared-error scaling laws linking spectral decay to convergence times and error curves.
Reports experimental confirmation of the predicted phases and exponents.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors characterize scaling laws in nonlinear regression with anisotropic data and identify how anisotropy reshapes learning dynamics, describing this as the first rigorous characterization of its kind.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the reduction yields a three-phase trajectory: rapid escape from low alignment, slow convergence of summary statistics, and subsequent learning in low-variance spectral directions.
The authors report explicit mean-squared-error scaling laws whose convergence times and error curves depend on spectral decay.
Experiments are reported to confirm the predicted phases and exponents.

narrative_sequence.summary: Frames scaling laws as a central learning-dynamics question and studies phase retrieval under power-law anisotropic Gaussian data.
Contrasts the isotropic two-dimensional dynamics with the anisotropic infinite hierarchy of coupled equations.
Introduces a tractable reduction exposing three sequential learning phases.
Uses the phase decomposition to derive mean-squared-error scaling laws governed by spectral decay.
Reports experimental agreement with predicted phases and exponents and positions the result as a first rigorous characterization.

source_observation.claim: The abstract organizes its dynamics through a three-phase decomposition and then derives error scaling laws from that decomposition.

lessons.interpretation: A staged mechanism can make a complex learning-curve claim more interpretable by connecting distinct dynamical regimes to measurable scaling behavior.
lessons.application: For a dynamics paper, define regime-specific phases first, then state which observable and scaling law each phase explains.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when phases cannot be separated operationally or when the target phenomenon is not sequential.

unknowns: The abstract gives no numerical exponents, convergence-time formulas, spectral-decay conditions, or parameter ranges.
Experimental setup, datasets, baselines, and quantitative agreement measures are unspecified.
The reduction’s assumptions and the precise meaning of “rigorous characterization” are not provided.
